title: An orbit is continuous falling
target: Explain a circular orbit with gravity and sideways motion.
criteria: Describe orbit as free fall rather than absent gravity.
Distinguish tangent velocity from inward force.
Connect circular speed to orbital radius.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: Why does an ideal satellite orbit a planet?
options: A constant outward force cancels gravity in an inertial frame.
It is beyond all gravitational influence.
It continually falls while moving sideways around the planet.
cpa.guide: Gravity bends the path while tangential motion carries it around the planet.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A satellite follows a circular orbit at constant speed. Is it accelerating?
options: No; gravity cannot act in orbit.
Yes; its velocity direction continually changes.
cpa.guide: Velocity changes direction, requiring inward acceleration.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: At the top of a counterclockwise circular orbit, which pair is correct?
options: Velocity left; gravity down toward the center.
cpa.guide: The tangent is left for counterclockwise motion; the center is below.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: If gravity suddenly vanished in an ideal orbit, what would happen immediately after?
options: The object would continue along the instantaneous tangent at constant velocity.
It would fly radially outward from rest.
It would keep curving at the same rate with no force.
cpa.guide: Without net force, velocity remains the tangent velocity at release.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: For a given central mass, circular speed is √(GM/r). What happens if orbital radius quadruples?
cpa.guide: The inverse square root of 4 is 1/2.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A student claims a larger circular orbit requires greater speed because the path is longer. Which correction is supported by gravity?
options: Every orbit has the same period.
Circular speed decreases with radius; period also depends on path length.
cpa.guide: v = √(GM/r); longer circumference does not imply faster motion.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
